title: West Fire Island: Native Coastal Homeland, Private Parcels and Federal Ownership
summary: West Fire Island belongs to a living Native coastal homeland. Records of company parcels and federal acquisition show later control of the island; public conservation ownership is not the same as returning Indigenous land or jurisdiction.
address_label: West Fire Island, Great South Bay — modern island context
map_geometry_source: Modern project coastline; National Park Service 2015 Map 3-C and GNIS 969221 geographic cross-check. Not a historical deed survey.
why_this_matters: Private subdivision and government conservation are different forms of land control. Neither makes the Native history of this coast disappear, nor establishes that land or authority was returned to a Native nation.
introduction_content: West Fire Island belongs to a living Native coastal homeland. Records of company parcels and federal acquisition show later control of the island; public conservation ownership is not the same as returning Indigenous land or jurisdiction.
history_title: From private parcels to federal ownership
history_content:
Which island is this?

West Fire Island is a small island in Great South Bay, northeast of Saltaire on the outer barrier beach. It lies between Sexton Island and East Fire Island. It is separate from the long ocean-facing Fire Island barrier and from places called West Island on Long Island’s North Shore. Fire Island Draft General Management Plan / Environmental Impact Statement: Map 3-C, Transportation

A coastal homeland before private parcels

The National Park Service places Fire Island and its waters within the long history of Unkechaug, Secatogue and Shinnecock people. Seasonal settlement, harvesting and care for coastal places preceded colonial settlement. Native stewardship continues today, including the Unkechaug community at Poospatuck. This regional history establishes the wider setting; it does not identify a particular village on West Fire Island. Native American Heritage at Fire Island National Seashore

Companies made the island into property parcels

A 1922 survey cited in the National Park Service’s historic study recorded Great South Bay Island Company holdings on West Island. Islip’s 1932 tax assessment rolls also recorded West Island Development Corporation parcels. These records make the later owners and the subdivision process visible: an island landscape was being administered as separate pieces of taxable and marketable property. Historic Resource Study: Fire Island National Seashore, Long Island, N.Y.

Federal acquisition changed the owner

The study identifies 1969 Department of the Interior taking files for West Island at the Suffolk County Clerk, including Index 179332. It describes government ownership and limits on further construction as conditions at the time of writing in 1979. These are documented later changes in control, not evidence of a seventeenth-century Native sale. Historic Resource Study: Fire Island National Seashore, Long Island, N.Y.

What the ownership trail does not settle

The records cited here do not establish the date, parties or terms of a Native conveyance of this particular island. Mainland deeds and the separately documented Captree, Oak and Grass litigation cannot simply be copied onto it. The outline locates the later ownership history; it does not certify an unbroken chain of title or the end of Native rights. Historic Resource Study: Fire Island National Seashore, Long Island, N.Y.

Public land and LandBack ask different questions

A government acquisition transfers control into a public institution. LandBack asks about Indigenous authority, access and relationships with land and water. Those are different outcomes: the acquisition described here is not documented as a return to a Native nation. The continuing Native stewardship described by the National Park Service is a starting point for considering whose knowledge and authority guide care for this coast. Native American Heritage at Fire Island National Seashore

Continue with Native objections to the outer beach’s colonial estate claims, the distinct Captree island dispute, and Unkechaug life at Poospatuck.
whereintheworld_content: This outline follows the project’s modern West Fire Island coastline for historical orientation. The island’s identity and position were checked against National Park Service Map 3-C and the published GNIS location. It is not a Native deed boundary, a reconstruction of the 1922 parcels, or the limits of the 1969 taking. Changing marsh edges and submerged property are not represented as a single historical acreage. The map is for learning; it does not identify a landing place or grant access.
